// version: 1.0. The criterion was set before it was met, and the evidence now covers the
code this actually ships.
1.0 is the claim that the shape survived contact with a SECOND implementation.
DemoViewer.NET implemented the contract over its own EntityState/EntityTracker
runtime against 0.1.1 -- no contract change required, no runtime hooks added,
43 conformance tests passing (SDK#6). That met the criterion on 0.1.1 and 1.0
was still withheld, because their findings had since changed the reference
reader: TryReadEntityHandle folds integral widths rather than converting them,
so a handle written as int -1 reads as the 0xFFFFFFFF sentinel instead of
absent. They had validated the reader BEFORE that change. Cutting 1.0 there
would have asserted the very thing the criterion exists to establish, on
evidence that did not cover it.
They re-ran against 0.2.1 and said so narrowly enough to act on:
https://github.com/CS2OpenDev/CS2OpenDev-SDK/issues/6#issuecomment-5288717770
-- the conformance port executed inside a full Parser suite run, 268/268
passed, 0 failed, 0 SKIPPED, so nothing passed by being skipped rather than
updated. Their handle-sentinel test asserts present-0xFFFFFFFF on a negative
integral write and predates the reference fix, which is why the reference
catching up moved nothing on their side. The only -1 literal in the port is an
out-of-range ORDINAL case that still reads absent, as the contract requires.
The remaining gap was that their word is against 0.2.1 and the published
release is 0.3.0. It closes by inspection rather than by argument:
git diff --stat CS2OpenDev.Sdk.Entities.Abstractions/v0.2.1 \
..CS2OpenDev.Sdk.Entities.Abstractions/v0.3.0 \
-- src/CS2OpenDev.Sdk.Entities.Abstractions/
-> version.json | 21 ++++-   (1 file changed)
0.3.0 was 94c3f64b, the versionHeightOffset cut, and it touched this file and
nothing else in this directory. No reader code, no interface, no conformance
kit moved between what they validated and what 1.0.0 carries. Had that diff
shown a single line of contract, the honest move would have been another 0.x
and another round -- the check is cheap and it is the whole discipline.
1.0 rather than 0.3.1 because 1.0 is a claim, not a patch. Mechanically the
MAJOR.MINOR bump also clears the height trap: editing this file restarts the
git height, so holding at 0.3 would have resolved 0.3.0 -- equal to what is
already published. See versionHeightOffset below.
What 1.0 obliges from here: a breaking change to this contract costs a MAJOR.
That is not free. SDK#30 (wrapper inheritance) has candidate resolutions that
would move the read seam off ordinal addressing, and if one of those is chosen
it ships as 2.0 rather than sliding in. Pricing that correctly is the point of
cutting 1.0, not an argument against it -- SDK#34 records that #30 is not a
gate for this release.
What 1.0 does NOT claim: that the contract is finished, or that a third
implementation would find nothing. It claims the shape held when someone other
than its author built against it, which is the only thing this repo can
honestly assert about a contract on its own.
It does NOT track the family major. Sdk, Sdk.GameEvents and Protos share a
major because they are one product regenerated together; this is a contract
with its own life, and pinning it to the schema's major would mean a Valve
patch could bump the version of a file nobody touched. The family went 4.1 ->
5.0 while this sat at 0.1.1, which is the arrangement working.
// versionHeightOffset: Cancels the commit that changes `version` above, so a MAJOR.MINOR bump cuts a
Nerdbank.GitVersioning counts height from the commit that last changed
`version`, and that commit is itself height 1 -- so the first release of every
new MAJOR.MINOR landed as .1 and no .0 has ever existed here. 22 released
versions, zero ending in .0. Shipping `5.0.1` as the first 5.0 implies a 5.0.0
that was superseded, which never existed.
This MUST be introduced alongside a MAJOR.MINOR bump. Adding it mid-stream
shifts the next resolved version DOWN by one, which can land below what is
already on the feed -- exactly the trap CS2OpenDev.Sdk.GameEvents' positive
offset was created to escape, in the other direction.
Cannot make height negative in practice: the offset only applies from the
commit that sets it, which is a `version` change, so height is at least 1.
// pathFilters: Its own directory and nothing else — this is the load-bearing line in the
file. Every other package here moves when the schema moves, because their
content is regenerated from it. A contract assembly that regenerates every
four hours is not frozen, whatever its documentation claims.
